zuint

Overview

R has 32-bit integers and doubles, and a double is exact only up to 253. Databases and data files have more: Arrow and Parquet have signed and unsigned 64-bit integers, and DuckDB adds 128-bit ones. Read into R, an unsigned ID or a HUGEINT becomes a double and quietly loses its low digits, and writing it back loses the column’s type as well.

zuint gives R the four integer types those engines use, int64, uint64, int128 and uint128, and moves them in and out of Arrow, Parquet and DuckDB with every value and every column type intact.

  • Exact or explicit. A result is exact, or it is NA with a warning, or an error. Nothing is rounded, truncated or clamped without saying so, and nothing is compared through a double.
  • Overflow is a choice. Operators give NA with a warning, as R’s integers do; checked_*() functions raise an error and wrapping_*() functions compute modulo 264 or 2128.
  • Types mix without loss. Combining two types gives the smallest type that holds both, so int64 and uint64 meet in int128; where there is no such type, it is an error.
  • Compatible with bit64. int64 is a bit64 integer64 underneath, so data.table, arrow, duckdb and the database drivers read it as they read integer64.
  • One bridge to the engines. Data moves through the Arrow C Data Interface, in C, with no R package in between; nanoarrow, arrow and duckdb are only needed for their own conveniences.
Engine type R today zuint
Arrow int64, DuckDB BIGINT a double by default, or bit64 integer64 int64
Arrow uint64, DuckDB UBIGINT a double, rounded beyond 253 uint64
DuckDB HUGEINT a double int128
DuckDB UHUGEINT a double uint128

Installation

zuint is not on CRAN yet. Install the development version from GitHub:

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("pedrobtz/zuint")

Usage 

library(zuint)

A number beyond 253 is exact, where a double has already rounded it:

x <- uint64("18446744073709551614")
x
#> <uint64[1]>
#> [1] 18446744073709551614
x - 1L
#> <uint64[1]>
#> [1] 18446744073709551613
sprintf("%.0f", 18446744073709551614 - 1)
#> [1] "18446744073709551616"

An out-of-range result is NA with a warning, unless you choose another overflow policy:

big <- int64("9223372036854775807")
big + 1L
#> Warning in Ops.zu_int64(big, 1L): 1 result is out of range. NA produced.
#> <int64[1]>
#> [1] NA
try(checked_add(big, 1L))
#> Error in checked_add(big, 1L) : 1 result is out of range.
wrapping_mul(x, 31L)
#> <uint64[1]>
#> [1] 18446744073709551554

Mixing types never loses a value: an int64 and a uint64 give an int128, and a product too large for int64 fits in int128:

int64(-1) + uint64("18446744073709551614")
#> <int128[1]>
#> [1] 18446744073709551613
int128(big) * 4L
#> <int128[1]>
#> [1] 36893488147419103228

Values come out of DuckDB as they are stored, and go back with their types. Here a UHUGEINT near the top of its range makes the round trip:

con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
ids <- zu_duckdb_query(
  con,
  "SELECT 340282366920938463463374607431768211454::UHUGEINT AS id"
)
ids$id
#> <uint128[1]>
#> [1] 340282366920938463463374607431768211454

zu_duckdb_register(con, "ids_back", ids)
DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT typeof(id) AS type, id::VARCHAR AS id FROM ids_back")
#>       type                                      id
#> 1 UHUGEINT 340282366920938463463374607431768211454
DBI::dbDisconnect(con)

Text goes both ways in decimal, hexadecimal and binary:

format_hex(uint64("0xdead_beef"))
#> [1] "0xdeadbeef"
format_bin(int64(-5))
#> [1] "-0b101"
format(int64(1234567890123), big.mark = ",")
#> [1] "1,234,567,890,123"

The constructors are named after the types, and every conversion into a type, from a double, a string or another type, follows the same rule: exact, or NA with a warning.

Performance

zuint’s int64 against bit64’s integer64 on random values across the whole range, in milliseconds (median of five runs; R 4.6.1, bit64 4.8.2, an Apple M-series laptop, 2026-10-16). match is zu_match(), the fast counterpart of base match(). The script is inst/bench/bench.R.

Elements Operation zuint bit64 zuint / bit64
106 + 2.9 11.1 0.26
sum 0.5 0.6 0.83
sort 13.7 14.8 0.93
match 11.9 10.5 1.13
unique 10.8 10.5 1.03
107 + 27 78 0.35
sum 5 6 0.83
sort 141 158 0.89
match 148 295 0.50
unique 147 283 0.52
108 + 266 781 0.34
sum 51 58 0.88
sort 2364 2339 1.01
match 3056 1579 1.94
unique 4148 1556 2.67

zuint is faster or level on most of them. It is slower for match and unique at 108 values, where its hash table outgrows memory caches, and slightly slower for match at 106.

Learn more

  • vignette("zuint") walks through the types, the promotion order, the overflow policies and the engine round trip.
  • The reference index lists every function, with the type ranges in ?int64, the overflow policies in ?checked_add and the Arrow bridge in ?zu_from_arrow.

Related work

bit64 gave R its 64-bit integers and the integer64 layout that zuint’s int64 keeps. The 128-bit arithmetic, parsing and formatting come from zufast. Arrow arrays move through the Arrow C Data Interface, and the 128-bit types through DuckDB’s arrow.opaque extension types. The tests check values against gmp.
